beats.intro: Chapter twelve. [[sub]]Everything so far leads here: putting a value on a share. This chapter introduces the main valuation tools.
beats.mispriced: Valuation compares an estimate of intrinsic value with the market price. [[val]]Say the analyst estimates the value at ten dollars. [[under]]If the shares trade at five, they look undervalued. [[fair]]At ten, fairly valued. [[over]]At twenty, overvalued. [[conf]]In practice, confidence matters. If the model or the inputs are uncertain, the analyst should demand a wide gap between value and price before acting. A ten dollar estimate against a ten oh five price is not a signal.
beats.models: Valuation models fall into three families. [[pv]]Present value models: discount expected future payoffs, such as dividends or free cash flow to equity. They are rooted in fundamentals, but sensitive to the inputs. [[mult]]Multiplier models: compare a price or enterprise value with a fundamental like earnings or sales, against peers. Simple and quick, but they inherit mispricing of the comparables. [[asset]]Asset-based models: value the assets, then subtract the liabilities. Useful when assets are tangible and measurable. [[note]]Each has strengths and weaknesses. Analysts often use several.
beats.dividends: Dividends are the cash flows behind many models. [[types]]A regular dividend is paid on a schedule. An extra dividend is a one-off. A stock dividend pays in new shares. A stock split divides each share into more, and a reverse split combines them. Neither changes the company's value. A repurchase buys shares back, returning cash to those who sell. [[chron]]The payment follows a chronology. On the declaration date, the board announces the dividend. [[ex]]On the ex-dividend date, new buyers no longer receive it, and the price typically drops by about the dividend. [[rec]]The holder of record date identifies who is paid. [[pay]]And the payment date is when cash is sent.
beats.pv: The logic of present value models is simple. [[eq]]A share is a claim on future cash flows. Its value is the present value of all expected dividends, discounted at the required return. [[pref]]Preferred stock is the easy case. It pays a fixed dividend forever. Five dollars a year, discounted at eight percent, is worth five over point oh eight: sixty two fifty. [[note]]For common stock, dividends are uncertain and may grow, so we need a growth assumption.
beats.gordon: The Gordon growth model assumes dividends grow at a constant rate forever. Value equals next year's dividend, divided by the required return minus the growth rate. [[base]]This year's dividend is two dollars. Growth is four percent, so next year's is two oh eight. With a nine percent required return, value is two oh eight over point oh five: forty one sixty. [[sens]]It is very sensitive. At an eight percent required return, the value is fifty two. At ten percent, thirty four sixty seven. At five percent growth, fifty two fifty. [[g]]Growth comes from reinvestment: retention rate times return on equity. Retaining forty percent, at a ten percent return, gives four percent. [[impl]]The model can also be turned around. If the price is forty one sixty, the required return implied is the dividend yield of five percent, plus growth of four, which is nine.
beats.twostage: Gordon growth suits stable companies. For a company that grows fast now and slows later, use a multistage model. [[hi]]Say dividends grow ten percent for three years: two twenty, two forty two, and two sixty six. [[pvs]]Discounted at nine percent, these are worth about two dollars each. [[tv]]After year three, growth settles at four percent. The terminal value at year three is the next dividend, two sixty eight, over point oh five: fifty five thirty seven. Discounted back, forty two seventy six. [[sum]]Total value: forty eight eighty seven. [[note]]Most of the value sits in the terminal value, so the long-run assumptions matter most.
beats.multiples: Multiples are the quick alternative. [[pe]]Price to earnings: a price of sixty, on earnings of four, is fifteen times. [[comp]]Compare with comparable companies. If peers trade at eighteen times, the implied value is seventy two, which suggests the share is undervalued. [[just]]Fundamentals explain multiples. The justified forward price to earnings ratio is the payout ratio, divided by required return minus growth. With a sixty percent payout, nine percent required return, and four percent growth, that is twelve. [[more]]Higher growth, or a lower required return, justifies a higher multiple. Other price multiples are price to book, price to sales, and price to cash flow.
beats.ev: Enterprise value multiples look at the whole firm. [[ev]]Enterprise value is market capitalization, plus debt and preferred stock, minus cash. Eight hundred, plus three hundred, minus one hundred: one thousand. [[mult]]With EBITDA of one twenty five, enterprise value to EBITDA is eight times. [[peer]]If comparable companies trade at ten times, the implied enterprise value is twelve fifty. [[eq]]Subtract debt, and add back cash, and equity is worth ten fifty. That is above the market capitalization of eight hundred, which suggests undervaluation. It is useful when capital structures differ.
beats.asset: Asset-based valuation starts from the balance sheet. [[assets]]Take assets with a book value of one thousand, but a fair market value of thirteen hundred. [[liab]]Liabilities are six hundred. [[eqv]]Equity is worth seven hundred, or seven dollars on one hundred shares. [[note]]This works best for companies with tangible, measurable assets, or in liquidation. It works poorly when value comes from intangibles and future earnings, which are hard to put on a balance sheet.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Compare intrinsic value with price, and require a wider gap when confidence is lower. [[w2]]Present value models discount dividends or cash flows. Gordon growth is value equals next dividend over required return minus growth. [[w3]]Multiples, including enterprise value multiples, compare firms quickly, but depend on the comparables. [[w4]]Asset-based models value assets minus liabilities, and fit asset-heavy companies.
beats.finish: That completes chapter twelve, and the book.
